$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces and let $k$ be a field. Inverse image of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, where $Rf_*$ is computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective replacements ([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]], [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]). For bounded complexes $A,B$ ([[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]) the derived tensor over $k$ is their signed total tensor ([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]), and for bounded $A$ and bounded-below $B$ the derived internal Hom $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ is computed by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ in a $k$-linear bounded-below injective model $B\to I_B$ ([[def-sheaf-hom]], [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]). Flasque $k$-sheaves ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) are acyclic for sections on every open set ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The tensor-Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, evaluation and symmetry identities are natural. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made here; that requires the local geometric supplier of the later constructible items.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); this covers in particular every sheaf
of $k$-vector spaces over a field $k$, which is the case used by the
compact-support calculus, and for such a sheaf the groups below are $k$-vector
spaces and the maps $k$-linear. Global sections are written
$\Gamma(X,-)$ ([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]). For a compact subset
$K\subseteq X$ ([[def-compact-space]]) let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion and consider the canonical restriction map
$$\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K),\qquad s\longmapsto s|_K,$$
which sends a global section ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]) to
the section of the inverse image sheaf ([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]])
that it induces on $K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is **c-soft**, also **soft for
compact supports**, when this map is surjective for every compact subset
$K\subseteq X$, that is: every section of $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset of
$X$ extends to a global section of $\mathcal F$. For sheaves of abelian groups
$\Gamma_c$ and $H^q_c$ of
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]] are the compactly supported
analogues of $\Gamma$ and $H^q$.

Two consistency facts hold; both are immediate from the definitions and from
the extension lemma for sections on a compact set, and they are recorded here
because the compact-support calculus uses the first constantly and the second
for injective sheaves.

1. **Neighbourhood formulation.** By
   [[lem-sections-near-a-compact-set-are-sections-on-that-set]], the source of
   the restriction map may be replaced by the defining colimit of the
   inverse-image presheaf,
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)=\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K}\mathcal F(U)$, so that
   $\mathcal F$ is c-soft if and only if for every compact $K$ and every open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, every section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ agrees with a
   global section of $\mathcal F$ on some open neighbourhood of $K$. It
   therefore suffices, for c-softness, to test the extended sections only
   locally near $K$.
2. **Flasque implies c-soft.** If $\mathcal F$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) then $\mathcal F$ is c-soft: a class in
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$ is represented by a section $s$ over an open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, and flasqueness extends $s$ to a global section
   $t\in\mathcal F(X)$ with $t|_U=s$, so $t$ is a preimage of that class.

C-softness is a property of the pair $(X,\mathcal F)$ and not of the sheaf
alone: the compact subsets of the base space are part of the test. Nothing is
assumed about the support of the extended global sections, and c-softness is
not the same condition as flasqueness, only implied by it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. The **restriction of $\mathcal F$ to $U$** is
the inverse image sheaf
$$
\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F.
$$

For an open set $W \subseteq U$, one may identify $(\mathcal F|_U)(W)$ with
$\mathcal F(W)$: because $U$ is open in $X$, the set $W$ is also open in $X$,
and in the neighbourhood-colimit defining $j^{-1}\mathcal F$ the open set $W$
itself is a neighbourhood of $j(W)=W$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let
$\mathcal E$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces. Suppose that
$$H^1_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0\qquad\text{for every open subspace }V\subseteq X,$$
where $\mathcal E|_V$ is the restriction
([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]) and $H^1_c$ is the first
compactly supported cohomology ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]).
Then $\mathcal E$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]); more precisely, every
section of $\mathcal E$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a
compactly supported global section of $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if
$\mathcal E$ is c-soft, then
$H^q_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0$ for every $q>0$ and every open subspace
$V\subseteq X$. Hence c-softness of $\mathcal E$ is equivalent to
$R\Gamma_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)$ being concentrated in degree $0$ for every open
subspace $V\subseteq X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $X$ be a topological space. Then
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ has enough injectives, every abelian sheaf on $X$ admits an
injective resolution ([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]), and
the embeddings below supply one injective resolution datum
([[def-supplied-injective-resolution-datum]]) on the whole category
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$: for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ the datum assigns one
specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
built functorially from $\mathcal F$ with no further selection.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Let $X$ be a topological space. A sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
is **exact** when it is exact in the abelian category of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]], equivalently in the sense of
[[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]].

Thus a sequence
$$
\cdots\to \mathcal F_{i-1}\to \mathcal F_i\to \mathcal F_{i+1}\to\cdots
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F_i$ when the image sheaf of the first morphism equals
the kernel sheaf of the second.

The same language applies to $\mathcal O_X$-modules on a ringed space.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

after.quote:
Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). Then:

1. **A neighbourhood base of compact sets.** If $X$ is locally compact
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) and Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]), then
   every neighbourhood $N$ of a point $x \in X$ ([[def-neighbourhood-top]])
   contains a compact neighbourhood of $x$; so the compact neighbourhoods of $x$
   form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
2. **Heredity along open and closed subspaces.** If $X$ is locally compact and
   Hausdorff and $S \subseteq X$ is open, then the subspace $S$ is locally
   compact ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). If $X$ is locally compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed, then the subspace $F$ is locally compact; no
   Hausdorff hypothesis is used for this half.
3. **Shrinking inside an open set.** If $X$ is locally compact and Hausdorff,
   $O \subseteq X$ is open and $x \in O$, there is an open $V$ with
   $$x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq O$$
   and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of $X$.
4. **Compact sets sit in open sets with compact closure.** If $X$ is locally
   compact and Hausdorff and $K \subseteq X$ is compact, there is an open
   $V \subseteq X$ with $K \subseteq V$ and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of
   $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**No choice principle is used**; every cover produced below is defined by a
formula and thinned by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns
members rather than indices.
The properties $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness are hereditary in the sense of [[def-hereditary-property]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); this covers in particular every sheaf
of $k$-vector spaces over a field $k$, which is the case used by the
compact-support calculus, and for such a sheaf the groups below are $k$-vector
spaces and the maps $k$-linear. Global sections are written
$\Gamma(X,-)$ ([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]). For a compact subset
$K\subseteq X$ ([[def-compact-space]]) let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion and consider the canonical restriction map
$$\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K),\qquad s\longmapsto s|_K,$$
which sends a global section ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]) to
the section of the inverse image sheaf ([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]])
that it induces on $K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is **c-soft**, also **soft for
compact supports**, when this map is surjective for every compact subset
$K\subseteq X$, that is: every section of $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset of
$X$ extends to a global section of $\mathcal F$. For sheaves of abelian groups
$\Gamma_c$ and $H^q_c$ of
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]] are the compactly supported
analogues of $\Gamma$ and $H^q$.

Two consistency facts hold; both are immediate from the definitions and from
the extension lemma for sections on a compact set, and they are recorded here
because the compact-support calculus uses the first constantly and the second
for injective sheaves.

1. **Neighbourhood formulation.** By
   [[lem-sections-near-a-compact-set-are-sections-on-that-set]], the source of
   the restriction map may be replaced by the defining colimit of the
   inverse-image presheaf,
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)=\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K}\mathcal F(U)$, so that
   $\mathcal F$ is c-soft if and only if for every compact $K$ and every open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, every section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ agrees with a
   global section of $\mathcal F$ on some open neighbourhood of $K$. It
   therefore suffices, for c-softness, to test the extended sections only
   locally near $K$.
2. **Flasque implies c-soft.** If $\mathcal F$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) then $\mathcal F$ is c-soft: a class in
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$ is represented by a section $s$ over an open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, and flasqueness extends $s$ to a global section
   $t\in\mathcal F(X)$ with $t|_U=s$, so $t$ is a preimage of that class.

C-softness is a property of the pair $(X,\mathcal F)$ and not of the sheaf
alone: the compact subsets of the base space are part of the test. Nothing is
assumed about the support of the extended global sections, and c-softness is
not the same condition as flasqueness, only implied by it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. The **restriction of $\mathcal F$ to $U$** is
the inverse image sheaf
$$
\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F.
$$

For an open set $W \subseteq U$, one may identify $(\mathcal F|_U)(W)$ with
$\mathcal F(W)$: because $U$ is open in $X$, the set $W$ is also open in $X$,
and in the neighbourhood-colimit defining $j^{-1}\mathcal F$ the open set $W$
itself is a neighbourhood of $j(W)=W$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let
$\mathcal E$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces. Suppose that
$$H^1_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0\qquad\text{for every open subspace }V\subseteq X,$$
where $\mathcal E|_V$ is the restriction
([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]) and $H^1_c$ is the first
compactly supported cohomology ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]).
Then $\mathcal E$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]); more precisely, every
section of $\mathcal E$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a
compactly supported global section of $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if
$\mathcal E$ is c-soft, then
$H^q_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0$ for every $q>0$ and every open subspace
$V\subseteq X$. Hence c-softness of $\mathcal E$ is equivalent to
$R\Gamma_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)$ being concentrated in degree $0$ for every open
subspace $V\subseteq X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $X$ be a topological space. Then
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ has enough injectives, every abelian sheaf on $X$ admits an
injective resolution ([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]), and
the embeddings below supply one injective resolution datum
([[def-supplied-injective-resolution-datum]]) on the whole category
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$: for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ the datum assigns one
specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
built functorially from $\mathcal F$ with no further selection.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Let $X$ be a topological space. A sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
is **exact** when it is exact in the abelian category of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]], equivalently in the sense of
[[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]].

Thus a sequence
$$
\cdots\to \mathcal F_{i-1}\to \mathcal F_i\to \mathcal F_{i+1}\to\cdots
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F_i$ when the image sheaf of the first morphism equals
the kernel sheaf of the second.

The same language applies to $\mathcal O_X$-modules on a ringed space.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Fix an open $U\subseteq X$, write $\mathcal O_U=\mathcal O_X|_U$ and $G_U:=j_{U!}\mathcal O_U$, the extension by zero of the structure sheaf restricted to $U$ [F5]. Its sections are $G_U(V)=\{a\in\mathcal O_X(V\cap U):\operatorname{Supp}(a)\text{ closed in }V\}$, and multiplication by $b\in\mathcal O_X(V)$ is $(b|_{V\cap U})a$; its support remains inside $\operatorname{Supp}(a)$, so this makes $G_U$ an $\mathcal O_X$-module. For $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ and $a\in G_U(V)$, the product $a\,s|_{V\cap U}$ is a section of $\mathcal F$ on $V\cap U$. On the open complement $V\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(a)$ take the zero section. The two sections agree on their overlap because $a$ vanishes there, so they glue uniquely to a section $\varphi_V(a)\in\mathcal F(V)$. This construction commutes with restriction and is $\mathcal O_X$-linear, hence defines $\varphi:G_U\to\mathcal F$ with $\varphi_U(1_U)=s$. Conversely, on $V\cap U$ any $\mathcal O_X$-linear morphism with this value sends $a$ to $a\,s|_{V\cap U}$, while on $V\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(a)$ it sends the zero section to zero; the same open cover therefore makes it unique. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)}(G_U,\mathcal F)\cong\mathcal F(U)$.

before.claim: **Fibres are locally compact Hausdorff.** For $y\in Y$ the fibre $F=f^{-1}(y)$ is closed in $X$ because $\{y\}$ is closed in the Hausdorff space $Y$ and $f$ is continuous [F1], so $F$ is a closed subspace of the locally compact space $X$ and is locally compact, and it is Hausdorff as a subspace of a Hausdorff space [F1]; the same holds for every open subspace $V\subseteq F$ [F1]. Consequently, for every sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $X$ that is c-soft on $X$, the restriction $\mathcal G|_F$ is c-soft on $F$ and its further restriction $\mathcal G|_V$ is c-soft on $V$, by the closed- and open-restriction clauses of [F2]; if $\mathcal G$ is injective on $X$ it is c-soft on $X$ by the injectivity clause of [F2].

**The resolution and its terms.** Fix the supplied functorial injective resolution datum on $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of [F4] (on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ for the abelian case) and let $0\to\mathcal A\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ be the injective resolution it assigns to $\mathcal A$. Each $I^j$ is injective in the chosen sheaf category, hence flasque and c-soft on $X$ by [F2], hence restricts to a c-soft sheaf $I^j|_F$ on every fibre $F$ and to a c-soft sheaf $I^j|_V$ on every open $V$ of a fibre, by [step 1.1]; in particular each $I^j$ is fibrewise c-soft.

**Dimension shifting on an open subspace of a fibre.** Let $V\subseteq F$ be open in a fibre $F=f^{-1}(y)$ and define the syzygies $Z^0:=\mathcal A$ and, for $j\ge0$, $Z^{j+1}:=\operatorname{coker}(Z^j\to I^j)$, so that $0\to Z^j\to I^j\to Z^{j+1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence of sheaves on $X$. Restricting to the open subspace $V$ preserves exactness and cokernels, so $0\to Z^j|_V\to I^j|_V\to Z^{j+1}|_V\to0$ is a short exact sequence of sheaves on the locally compact Hausdorff space $V$ [F5] whose middle term is c-soft, hence acyclic [F2]; the long exact compactly supported cohomology sequence of [F5] therefore gives isomorphisms $H^p_c(V,Z^{j+1}|_V)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{p+1}_c(V,Z^j|_V)$ for every $p\ge1$, because the two adjacent groups of the c-soft sheaf $I^j|_V$ vanish in positive degrees. Iterating these isomorphisms for $j=0,1,\dots,d-1$ with $p=1,2,\dots,d$ gives $H^1_c(V,Z^d|_V)\cong H^{d+1}_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)=0$, the last group vanishing by the dimension hypothesis of the statement because $d+1>d$ and $V$ is an open subspace of a fibre.

**The cokernel after $d$ steps is fibrewise c-soft.** Let $F=f^{-1}(y)$ be any fibre and let $V\subseteq F$ be open; by [step 3.1] one has $H^1_c(V,Z^d|_V)=0$ for every such $V$, so the vanishing criterion [F3] applied to the locally compact Hausdorff space $Z=F$ and the sheaf $\mathcal E=Z^d|_F$ shows that $Z^d|_F$ is c-soft on $F$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $Z^d$ restricts to a c-soft sheaf on every fibre. Concatenating the short exact sequences $0\to Z^j\to I^j\to Z^{j+1}\to0$ for $j=0,\dots,d-1$ gives the exact sequence $0\to\mathcal A\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\to I^{d-1}\to Z^d\to0$, a bounded resolution of $\mathcal A$ entirely by $k$-linear maps and $k$-sheaves (by abelian maps and sheaves in the abelian case), whose terms $I^0,\dots,I^{d-1}$ are fibrewise c-soft by [step 2.1] and whose last term $Z^d$ is fibrewise c-soft by the preceding argument; when $d=0$ the construction stops at $Z^0=\mathcal A$ and the isomorphism $H^1_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)\cong H^{d+1}_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)=0$ of [step 3.1] with $d=0$ gives the c-softness of $\mathcal A$ on every fibre directly by [F3].

The Axiom of Choice is used only through the injective resolution datum of [F4] and the delta-functor and comparison statements of [F5], whose connecting maps use dependent choice, a consequence of AC [F6]; the fibre-by-fibre dimension count of [step 3.1] is finite.

before.quote:
Assume AC. Let $f:X\to Y$ be one morphism of reduced quasi-projective complex
algebraic varieties, and prescribe finitely many closed or locally closed
algebraic subsets in source and target. There exist finite smooth complex
algebraic Whitney (a),(b) stratifications with frontier on $X$ and $Y$
respecting all prescribed subsets, such that each source stratum maps
surjectively and smoothly onto one target stratum. A further finite algebraic
stratification may be prescribed and refined. The analytic strata are smooth
complex manifolds and the restrictions are smooth submersions. If $f$ is proper
in the analytic topology, in particular if it is a projective algebraic
morphism, the whole restriction $f^{-1}(T)\to T$ over any target stratum is
proper; no restriction of $f$ to a nonclosed individual source stratum is
asserted proper.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety with
a finite smooth complex algebraic Whitney stratification. Its analytic
stratified space admits compatible tube control data. At every point $y$ of a
stratum $R$ there is a stratum-preserving neighborhood homeomorphism
$$U_y\cong B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c_{<1}(L_y),$$
where $L_y$ is a compact finitely Whitney-stratified real semialgebraic normal
link. The ball times cone apex is $R\cap U_y$, and upper strata correspond to
their link strata times positive radius and the ball. The local construction
can preserve a chosen ordinary normal projection and radius at $R$. Links are
locally constant in stratified homeomorphism type along $R$. Proper stratified
algebraic submersions, with their actual analytic properness, have whole-fiber
local stratified bundle trivializations; local submersions have
source-neighborhood products. No compatible triangulation or finite
sheaf-cochain model is assumed or asserted here.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, $k$ a
field, and $F$ a bounded complex of analytic $k$-sheaves whose cohomology is
locally constant of finite rank on a finite complex algebraic stratification.
Fix finitely many algebraic supports and locally closed inclusions to be
respected. There is a finite compatible smooth complex algebraic Whitney
refinement, a projective compactification with its algebraic boundary
respected, and a finite pair of simplicial complexes $(K,D)$ such that
$X^{\mathrm{an}}\cong|K|\setminus|D|$, every open simplex lies in one complex
stratum, and the marked supports are unions of simplices. One can take
$\dim K\le2\dim_{\mathbb C}X$; in particular constant-sheaf cohomology vanishes
above that real dimension. The same construction applies individually to the
compact controlled links supplied by the conical-neighborhood theorem.

On these models, actual ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary
derived Hom, internal derived Hom and local cohomology with a prescribed
algebraic support have bounded finite-dimensional cochain models. Internal Hom
is constructible on a finite complex Whitney refinement. The local link and
support models vary locally constantly along the corresponding complex strata;
thus their cohomology has finite rank there. Every such model commutes with
extension of the coefficient field. Inclusions and supports are chosen in
finite collections for a given construction; no compatible triangulation of
arbitrary algebraic maps or cyclic diagrams is asserted. Perverse dimensions
remain the dimensions of the complex strata, independent of the auxiliary real
simplices.

Assume AC. Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex, $D$ a subcomplex and $X=|K|\setminus|D|$. Let $P$ be the face poset of the open simplices of $K$ not in $D$, ordered by inclusion of faces. The exact realization of finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ induces a fully faithful functor into $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, with essential image the complexes having bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary Hom and internal derived Hom have bounded finite cochain models and commute with every coefficient field extension. For a local product projection $\operatorname{pr}:V\times F\to V$ with supplied finite deleted-boundary models, there is a natural local comparison $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, taking the unit to $B\otimes(k\to C^*(F;k))$. This does not assert that an arbitrary algebraic map is simplicial.

Assume AC. For a strict augmented simplicial space $Z_\bullet\to S$, its category of simplicial analytic $k$-sheaves has explicit coinduced injective resolutions. The derived augmentation is computed by the normalized double complex with first page $R^j q_{p*}F_p$ and alternating face differential. A common internal lower bound makes every total-degree diagonal finite. The same construction works for strict bisimplicial diagrams and is compatible with composition of derived right adjoints to exact inverse image. If $Z_\bullet$ is the Čech nerve of a map $P\to S$ admitting local sections, inverse image gives an equivalence from $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(S))$ to the full derived subcategory with Cartesian cohomology. For algebraic principal $\mathrm{GL}$ bundles this restricts to the algebraically constructible subcategories.

Let $k$ be a field and let $X,Y$ be locally compact Hausdorff spaces
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]). Write
$\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]])
viewed as modules over the constant ring sheaf $k_X$, and form derived
categories in those sheaves ([[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]).
For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$, set $f^*=f^{-1}$
([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) and define $f_!F$ on an open
$V\subseteq Y$ to consist of the sections of $F$ on $f^{-1}(V)$ whose closed
support ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]],
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]) maps properly to $V$, properness
being that of [[def-proper-continuous-map]] together with its stability lemma
[[lem-proper-continuous-map-stability]]. Under AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]),
$Rf_*$ and $Rf_!$ are computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective
replacements. Tensor means the signed total tensor over $k$
([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]) and internal derived Hom is the injective
construction of
[[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]]
([[def-sheaf-hom]]).

Suppose the uniform all-fibre-open cohomological dimension bound of
[[lem-finite-fibre-dimension-gives-bounded-fibrewise-soft-resolutions]] holds,
and choose its finite resolution $k_X\to K$; for an open $U\subseteq X$ put
$K_U=j_{U!}j_U^*K$ ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]],
[[def-c-soft-sheaf]]). For a bounded-below injective complex $I$ on $Y$,
define the exceptional inverse-image candidate to be the sheaf complex with
open sections $\operatorname{Hom}_Y^\bullet(f_!K_U,I)$.
[[thm-compactly-supported-derived-pushforward-has-exceptional-inverse-image-adjoint]]
proves that this candidate is a sheaf complex and is independent of the chosen
resolution. Set $\omega_X=a_X^!k$ and $D_XA=R\mathcal Hom(A,\omega_X)$ when the
terminal map satisfies the same finite-dimensional hypotheses. Constructible
restriction is a separate geometric theorem; none of these definitions asserts
a generic six-functor axiom.

The prescriptions are those of Verdier's exposé: $f^*$ is the exact inverse
image, $f_!$ is the sheaf of sections whose closed support is proper over the
base — a presheaf by the local nature of properness, whose sheaf property on
bounded-below injective inputs is proved by the exceptional-adjoint theorem
recorded in `justified_by` — $Rf_*$ is derived from the direct image
[[def-direct-image-sheaf]] on bounded-below injective replacements, and the
terms of the chosen finite resolution are $c$-soft and hence acyclic for
compact support ([[lem-c-soft-field-sheaves-are-compact-support-acyclic]]).
The ordinary-operations lemma also supplies the flasque acyclicity
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) used to compare resolutions. AC is used only for
injective replacements; the proper-support sections, extension by zero and the
exceptional candidate itself are choice-free constructions. Cohomological
shifts obey $H^i(A[r])=H^{i+r}(A)$ in the convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

Under the preceding locally compact and finite-dimensional hypotheses, $u^*Rf_!\simeq Rf'_!v^*$ for Cartesian squares; proper maps have $Rf_!=Rf_*$, giving proper ordinary base change. Bounded tensor factors satisfy the projection formula. Proper-support direct images compose canonically. On the bounded constructible specialization proved by the subsequent local duality construction, exceptional adjoints also compose canonically; their units, counits and traces respect composition and Cartesian pasting. For a closed inclusion $i:Z\to X$ with complement $j$, $i^!$ is the derived functor of $i^{-1}\Gamma_Z$, and both localization triangles hold. Locally, $R\mathcal Hom(i_*k_Z,A)$ is $R\Gamma_ZA$. This lemma does not assume or claim extraordinary dual base change before constructible biduality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P=|K|$ be the realization of a finite abstract
simplicial complex $K$ of dimension $d$ (a finite compact polyhedron of
dimension $d$), and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $P$
([[def-geometric-realization-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]],
[[def-locally-finite-and-finite-dimensional-simplicial-complex]],
[[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies to sheaves of
$k$-vector spaces. Then:

1. $H^q(P,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>d$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
2. for every open subspace $U\subseteq P$ and every sheaf $\mathcal E$ of
   abelian groups on $U$, one has $H^q_c(U,\mathcal E)=0$ for every $q>d$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]);
3. more generally, the same conclusions hold for every compact Hausdorff space
   in which every open cover admits a finite open refinement of order at most
   $d+1$ --- that is, a finite refinement such that every point lies in at most
   $d+1$ of its members --- and for every open subspace of such a space.

These bounds concern arbitrary sheaves, not merely cellular, constructible or
coherent ones. If $L\subseteq K$ is a subcomplex, then $|L|$ is closed in $P$,
the complement $P\setminus|L|$ is open, and every open subspace of
$P\setminus|L|$ is an open subspace of $P$; this is the fibre model on which
the bound is applied.
